passage: Francis here. I noticed something odd about Samir last week when we split up our project tasks. A new teammate, Tashi, had just joined from a small hill town. Samir was about to hand Tashi the easy formatting job. Samir's pen stopped, and then Samir laughed a little awkwardly and said to me, "Wait. Why did I assume Tashi couldn't handle the data part?" It was quiet for a second. I couldn't tell whether Samir felt embarrassed or curious. What I saw was that Samir didn't argue with the thought or brush it away. Samir asked Tashi to take the data analysis. Tashi did it faster than any of us and taught the rest of us a shortcut. Samir told me afterwards, "Good to check my guesses against actual people."

qa.q: Which task was Samir about to give Tashi?
qa.a: Samir was about to hand Tashi the easy formatting job.

qa.q: What might Samir have been feeling when Samir stopped and asked "Why did I assume...?"
qa.a: Possibly awkward or curious, since Samir laughed a little awkwardly, though Francis says Francis could not tell.

qa.q: What did Samir do that worked well?
qa.a: Samir noticed the assumption without brushing it away, then tested it by asking Tashi to take the data analysis.

qa.q: How might Tashi have felt about being given the data work?
qa.a: Tashi may have felt trusted and respected, as the result was work faster than anyone else's.

grounding: The protagonist catches an assumption about a teammate's origin, notices it without shame and tests it against the real person.

Day one. Bhupen's new roommate in the Guwahati hostel was Kamal, from a small town in Bihar. Before Kamal had even unpacked, Bhupen had decided: he'll be loud, messy, on the phone all night. Bhupen moved his own books to the top shelf.

Two weeks later. Bhupen caught himself again. When his laptop charger went missing, his first thought was Kamal. Then he found it in his own bag. His face went hot. Where had that thought come from? He'd grown up hearing uncles say things about "those people" at weddings. He had thought he was different.

A month in, a Sunday. Kamal woke him at seven, not with noise, but with tea, because Bhupen had an exam. Kamal was the tidiest person on the floor. That evening Bhupen told him, awkwardly, "I judged you before I knew you. I'm sorry." Kamal laughed. "Everyone does. You're the first to say it."

qa.q: Where did Bhupen find the missing charger?
qa.a: Bhupen found it in his own bag.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling when he found the charger?
qa.a: Bhupen felt ashamed and uncomfortable, his face going hot as he noticed his own bias.

qa.q: What did Bhupen do instead of denying his bias?
qa.a: Bhupen noticed the thought, questioned where it came from, compared it with the real Kamal and apologised honestly.

qa.q: How might Kamal see Bhupen's apology?
qa.a: Kamal seems to take it lightly and with some relief, since many people judge him but few admit it.

grounding: The three beats show a young man noticing his assumptions about someone from another region, testing them against the real person and learning.

passage:
Vaibhav, you asked me about prejudice, so let me tell you something I'm not proud of. I'm Santosh, and when I was twenty, at the textile mill in Surat, a new supervisor joined, Yusuf bhai. First day, I told my friends, "Watch, he'll only favour his own people." I didn't know one thing about him. Only his name.

For a month I watched him like a detective, waiting to be right. Every small thing, I counted as proof.

Then my mother fell ill and I needed three days' leave in peak season. Yusuf bhai gave me five, and covered my machine himself. I felt so small. Not because he was kind. Because I'd been so sure.

That's when I started asking myself: this idea in my head, is it about this man, or about something I heard as a boy? You'll have ideas like that too. Everyone does. Notice them. Check them.

qa.q: Where did Santosh work at twenty?
qa.a: Santosh worked at the textile mill in Surat.

qa.q: How did young Santosh feel when Yusuf bhai gave him leave?
qa.a: Young Santosh felt small and ashamed, realising how sure he had been without any real knowledge.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Santosh handled his assumptions?
qa.a: After Yusuf bhai's help, Santosh began asking whether a thought was about the real person or something heard as a boy.

qa.q: How might Yusuf bhai have felt being watched closely that first month?
qa.a: Yusuf bhai may have felt uneasy or judged, sensing suspicion from a worker who didn't know him.

grounding: The elder's story shows a young man assuming things about someone because of his religion, noticing the bias and testing it against the real person.
